paragraphs.heading: Who he was
paragraphs.text: Napoleon Bonaparte was a general who came to the fore during the French Revolution and later ruled France as its emperor. He held that title from 18 May 1804 until he first gave up the throne in 1814, and briefly again in 1815 during the period called the Hundred Days. He fought campaigns across Europe and the Middle East. As a statesman, he also brought in many legal and administrative reforms in France and the rest of Europe.

paragraphs.heading: A Corsican beginning
paragraphs.text: He was born on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio, on the island of Corsica, into a family of Italian origin. Corsica had passed to France from the Republic of Genoa just one year earlier. His father won the backing of the French governor, and with that help the young Napoleon received a royal grant to attend a military academy in mainland France. He moved there in 1779 and became an officer in the French Royal Army in 1785.

paragraphs.heading: Rise to power
paragraphs.text: Napoleon backed the Revolution in 1789. He climbed quickly after his success at the siege of Toulon in 1793 and his defeat of royalist rebels in Paris in 1795. In 1796 he led a campaign against Austria and its Italian allies, won decisive victories, and became a national hero. After invading Egypt and Syria in 1798, he organized the Coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799 and became First Consul of the Republic.

paragraphs.heading: Emperor and conqueror
paragraphs.text: Napoleon placed the crown on his own head in December 1804, taking the title Emperor of the French. When a new coalition of his enemies formed against him, he shattered it at the Battle of Austerlitz, which led to the end of the Holy Roman Empire. He beat Prussia at Jena–Auerstedt in 1806 and the Russians at Friedland in 1807. In 1808 he invaded the Iberian Peninsula and made his brother Joseph King of Spain, setting off the Peninsular War.

paragraphs.heading: Russia and the fall
paragraphs.text: In the summer of 1812 he invaded Russia and briefly held Moscow, but his army's retreat that winter was a disaster. In 1813 Prussia, Austria and Russia defeated him decisively at the Battle of Leipzig. They invaded France, took Paris and forced him to abdicate in April 1814, and he was sent into exile on Elba. Ten months later he escaped, took back control of France, and was defeated by yet another coalition at Waterloo in June 1815.

paragraphs.heading: Exile and death
paragraphs.text: After Waterloo he was exiled to Saint Helena, a remote island in the South Atlantic. He died there of stomach cancer in 1821, at the age of 51. Since then he has kept a prominent place in both historical research and popular culture.

paragraphs.heading: A mixed legacy
paragraphs.text: Napoleon is counted among history's greatest military commanders, and military schools around the world still study his tactics. His best-known reform is the Napoleonic Code. He set up public education, freed Jews and other religious minorities, and established equality before the law. Yet he also abolished the free press, jailed or exiled critics, brought back slavery in French colonies, and cut the rights of women and children, so he remains a controversial figure.
